source.title: DB-KSVD: Scalable Alternating Optimization for Disentangling High-Dimensional Embedding Spaces
source.authors: Romeo Valentin; Sydney M. Katz; Vincent Vanhoucke; M. Kochenderfer

record.tranche_reason: The study takes superposition and entangled embeddings as motivation for dictionary learning, but does not test whether individual neurons are polysemantic. Its reported semantic evaluations concern learned dictionary features.
record.gate_note: The study assumes a sparse superposition model and evaluates learned dictionary features, not individual neurons or neuron-level responses. It does not test any of V1–V7. The DINOv2 autointerpretability results below are related feature-level findings, not measurements of neuron polysemanticity.
record.test_reason: The study assumes the superposition hypothesis as motivation for dictionary learning and reports only its own method's (DB-KSVD) performance against SAEs on learned dictionary features. It never measures individual neurons or neuron-level polysemanticity, so no version V1–V7 is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that DB-KSVD scales KSVD to interpretability-sized problems and matches SAEs across SAEBench and DINOv2 metrics. They read this as a sign that both methods may be near the theoretical limits. They also find that Matryoshka structuring lowers coherence and, for m=4096, improves autointerpretability and absorption, while slightly lowering loss recovered and SCR. They say it is unclear whether the gains come from the dictionaries or from the sparse encoding.
record.recipe_differences: Not a replication of the neuron-level methods or claims in the cited original sources; it learns and evaluates sparse dictionaries of embedding features.

fits_no_version.finding: DINOv2 dictionary features from DB-KSVD score higher on VLM autointerpretability than TopK-SAE features at every sparsity, with a larger gap for DINOv2-S (d=384).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dictionary-learned features of vision transformer embeddings are interpretable, and alternating optimization matches or exceeds SAEs on feature-level autointerpretability; this is a feature-level, not neuron-level, result.

record.problems: The semantic evaluations are on learned dictionary features rather than individual neurons. Vision autointerpretability is a proxy based on GPT-4o-mini explanations and scoring over 100 top-variance features; no uncertainty estimates are reported for the tabulated scores.
record.rows_left_out: No results about neuron-level polysemanticity were reported. Other dictionary benchmark metrics, coherence results, and timing results were left out because they do not measure neuron polysemanticity or the semantic interpretability outcome recorded here.

untested.parts: No neurons in image classifiers are examined; DINOv2 CLS embeddings are decomposed into dictionary atoms.
No MLP neuron responses in Gemma-2-2B or Pythia-160M are measured; only layer-12 residual embeddings are decomposed.
Superposition is assumed as the generative model, not tested as a cause of neuron polysemanticity.
No test of polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization or noise under spare capacity.
Matryoshka structuring changes dictionary coherence, not the share of polysemantic neurons; no activation-function or architecture comparison.
No canonical polysemantic neurons are re-examined.
No neuron-level polysemanticity measure is compared across activation ranges or scoring methods.

record.verdict_notes: Pure dictionary-learning method paper. It cites superposition (Elhage et al.) only as motivation. No neuron-level data, so no verdicts are given. The reader's T4/assumes classification is correct.

versions.untested_parts: No individual neurons in image classifiers are measured or interpreted.
No transformer MLP neuron responses to tokens or contexts are measured.
Superposition is a motivating assumption; the study does not test whether capacity pressure causes neuron polysemanticity.
No neuron polysemanticity is measured in relation to initialization, regularization, or training noise under spare capacity.
Matryoshka structuring is applied to learned dictionaries, not tested for changing the share of polysemantic neurons; activation functions and neuron-level performance costs are not tested.
The study evaluates learned dictionary atoms, not canonical polysemantic neurons or whether their activations share a feature.
No neuron polysemanticity measure is compared across activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods.

rows.subject: DINOv2-S
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated autointerpretability of learned dictionary features using GPT-4o-mini explanations scored against held-out images.
rows.measure: Mean autointerpretability score; Spearman correlation of CLIP similarity between explanation and image with activation values.
rows.note: This scores learned dictionary features, not individual neurons; it does not determine whether neurons are polysemantic.
rows.check: Method-comparison row (DB-KSVD vs SAE dictionary features), not a neuron polysemanticity measurement. Values match Table 4.
